analysis.investment_thesis: Indo Count is a home textile exporter with decent revenue growth (~13% CAGR last 4 years) but zero profit compounding over nine years and rapidly rising debt eating into already thin margins. At 48x trailing P/E with ROE of only 11.3%, this business does not meet my bar for a high-conviction India growth bet.
key_strengths: Revenue trajectory improving: INR 4,151 Cr in FY25, up from INR 2,519 Cr in FY21, riding China+1 export tailwinds
Promoter holding stable at 58.74% with reasonable D/E of 0.54 — not a governance disaster
Forward P/E of 19.7x suggests market expects substantial earnings normalisation, offering optionality if margins recover
key_risks: Finance costs exploded 75% YoY (INR 70 Cr → INR 123 Cr), crushing net profit to INR 246 Cr vs INR 338 Cr prior year — debt trajectory is dangerous
Net profit CAGR of -0.2% over 9 years: a business that earns no more today than in 2016 is not compounding wealth
Operating margin of 4.86% is structurally thin in a commoditised, FX-sensitive export sector — no pricing power moat
red_flags: Net profit fell from INR 338 Cr (FY24) to INR 246 Cr (FY25) even as revenue grew 17% — operating leverage is negative
Total debt surged to INR 1,449 Cr in FY25 from INR 956 Cr (FY24) — a 51% jump in one year with no commensurate profit growth
OCF only positive in 3 of last 5 years; INR 485 Cr investing outflow in FY25 against INR 394 Cr OCF leaves almost no free cash buffer
48x trailing P/E for a commodity textile company with sub-12% ROE is unjustifiable — multiple contraction risk is high
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Indo Count's nine-year story is one of cyclical lurches rather than compounding: net profit in FY25 (INR 246 Cr) is actually below FY16 levels (INR 251 Cr) despite revenue nearly doubling. The FY22 peak of INR 359 Cr is already a distant memory, and FY25 marks a second consecutive cycle of profit erosion. What killed FY25 earnings is clear — finance costs of INR 123 Cr vs INR 70 Cr in FY24, driven by a borrowings surge from INR 956 Cr to INR 1,243 Cr. When a business is growing revenue at 13-17% per year but its interest bill grows 75% in a single year, the capital allocation discipline must be questioned.

From my perspective, textiles are a sector I would only back if there is a dominant brand moat, spectacular return ratios, or a structural government policy kicker that creates durable advantage. Indo Count has none of these in strong enough form. ROE at 11.3% and ROCE at 13.5% are well below my 20%+ threshold for high conviction. The gross margin of 52% looks impressive but evaporates entirely by the operating margin line to just 4.86%, implying the company is a price-taker in its end markets. The forward P/E of 19.7x tells me the market is baking in a sharp earnings recovery — possible if cotton costs ease and US retail demand firms up — but that is a trade, not an investment. I do not build concentrated positions on cyclical recoveries in low-ROE businesses.
